Q: Late binding in Racket Scheme can't be found in a let-environment A:

Answering your follow-up questions:

define inside a function is called internal definition. The R5RS standard only specifies that implementations must support consecutive internal definitions that appear at the beginning (that is, not interrupted by expressions).

Your first follow-up example, however, doesn't have all internal definitions at the beginning consecutively. (define var 9) is interrupted by the expression (g).

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (g)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g))

(f)

Many R5RS implementations simply reject this program as syntactically ill-formed. Try e.g. https://ideone.com/ on Guile.

Racket implementation of R5RS chooses to support this "unrestricted internal definition", but since the standard doesn't say how it should work, there are many possible ways to support it. Racket R5RS goes with one possible behavior: it groups a sequence of consecutive internal definitions together, and break groups into different scopes where a group can refer to definitions in groups preceding it, but not the other way around. I.e., the program is essentially transformed to:

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (g)
  (let ()
    (define var 9)
    (display "---") (newline)
    (g)))

(f)

where var in g always refers to the outermost var. This is why it prints 6 .... 6.

In your second follow-up example, (define var 9) is not interrupted, so it follows the standard R5RS semantics, where var in g always refers to var in (define var 9). This is why it prints 9.

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  ;(g)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g)
  )

(f)

The actual Racket language (not R5RS) also supports unrestricted internal definition, but with a different behavior from Racket R5RS. var in g always refers to var in (define var 9).

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (g)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g))

(f)

However, the association of the value 9 to var only occurs when the statement is evaluated. Initially, var is uninitialized. Since (g) is called when var is still uninitialized, the evaluation of var results in the runtime error "cannot use before initialization", as you observed.

Using what I described above, we can see that:

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (+ 1 1)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g))

(f)

in Racket R5RS would print 6, since (define var 9) is broken up by (+ 1 1), making it effectively transformed to:

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (+ 1 1)
  (let ()
    (define var 9)
    (display "---") (newline)
    (g)))

(f)

But the same program in Racket would print 9, since var in g refers to var in (define var 9), which is already associated with the value 9 by the time g is called.

Q: Calling Fortran intrinsics in gdb A:

some intrinsics are defined in gdb (see for instance https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Fortran-Intrinsics.html), suppose x defined by

 x = [(i*i, i=1, 10)]

then p size(x) gives you 10. If you need more complex intrinsic like maxval you could use

the pretty printer from mankoff (https://github.com/mankoff/gdb_fortran_tools) using numpy command directly in fortran like np max x

Q: Gitlab CI pipeline rules seems not take into account variables set during pipeline execution A:

This is exactly the documented behaviour in the docs https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/yaml/#rules

Rules are evaluated when the pipeline is created, and evaluated in order.

GitLab pipeline process evaluates the rules at pipeline creation to know which jobs to create. Since at the time of pipeline creation there is no variable called APP_VERSION then this correctly doesn't match your regex.

If you want to check it at run time then check it in the script block as shell code.

Q: How to get the marked answer from a OMR Sheet? A:

Here is one way in Python OpenCV.

Since the OP did not provide an original image, I have to start with the image that was provided with the green boxes and remove them.

  • Read the input image

  • Crop to remove red at the borders

  • Threshold on the green boxes as a mask and use that mask to set the image to white for for mask value of 255

  • Convert to grayscale as gray (and a second version, gray2, as float in the range 0 to 1 and third version, gray3, as 3-channel version of gray)

  • Threshold on gray and invert as thresh and make a version, thresh2, as float in the range 0 to 1

  • Get contours

  • Find the contours' center x and y values

  • Compute the mean of the center x and y values to form grid line x and y value

  • Print the number of rows and columns from the grid lines x and y values

  • Find the marked answers using a threshold on the area of the inside region of the contours in the gray2 image

  • Compute the grid line indices (starting from 1) for the found answers. Also convert index 10 to index 0, since the OMR image has circles inscribing numerical labels with row 0 after 9 rather 10

  • Print Table 1 as a list of the found answer's x and y centers

  • Print Table 2 with the found answer x and y centers and their row and column indices sorted by column first then row.

  • Print a simple comma delimited list of the row values

Input image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input image
img = cv2.imread('OMR4.png')

# crop image to remove red border
img2 = img[2:-1, 1:-1]

# remove the green boxes
low = (0,128,0)
high = (0,128,0)
green_mask = cv2.inRange(img2, low, high)
img2[green_mask==255] = (255,255,255)

# convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img2, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# scale gray image to a float range between 0.0 to 1.0
if gray.max() > 1:
    gray2 = gray.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
else:
    gray2 = gray.copy().astype(np.float32)

# convert gray to a 3 channel version, gray3
gray3 = cv2.cvtColor(gray, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)

# threshold and invert gray image and create version thresh2 in float range (0.0 to 1.0)
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)[1]
thresh2 = thresh.astype(np.float32) / 255.0

# get contours from the thresh image
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_NONE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]

# initialize a mask filled with zeros (black)
mask = np.zeros(gray2.shape[:2], dtype=np.uint8)

# define threshold value and gap tolerance values
threshold_value = 0.7  # values smaller than this for the mean in gray2 become "found answers"
fraction = 0.4  # multiplies the median gap as the tolerance
min_tolerance = 5
fallback_tolerance = 10

# align x and y values to their mean values from the save centers to form unique 
# column and row x and y values. That is form grids lines.
def cluster_coordinates_auto(coords):
    # sort the list of x or y coordinates as provided from smallest to largest
    sorted_coords = sorted(coords)
    if not sorted_coords:
        return []
    
    # compute the differences between adjacent x or y coordinates
    diffs = np.diff(sorted_coords)
    
    # trap for 1 point, i.e. 0 pairs, then return the original sorted x or y 
    if len(diffs) == 0:
        return [int(sorted_coords[0])]
    
    # filter out zero or near-zero differences since coordinates are too close
    non_zero_diffs = [d for d in diffs if d > 1]
    
    if non_zero_diffs:
        tolerance = max(min_tolerance, int(np.median(non_zero_diffs) * fraction))
    else:
        tolerance = fallback_tolerance  # Fallback default

    clusters = [[sorted_coords[0]]]
    for val in sorted_coords[1:]:
        if val - clusters[-1][-1] <= tolerance:
            clusters[-1].append(val)
        else:
            clusters.append([val])
            
    return [int(np.mean(c)) for c in clusters]

# extract contour centers and build a full set of grid lines
all_contour_x = []
all_contour_y = []

for contour in contours:
    M = cv2.moments(contour)
    if M["m00"] != 0:
        cX = int(M["m10"] / M["m00"])
        cY = int(M["m01"] / M["m00"])
        all_contour_x.append(cX)
        all_contour_y.append(cY)

# compute grid lines using all detected contours
grid_lines_x = cluster_coordinates_auto(all_contour_x)
grid_lines_y = cluster_coordinates_auto(all_contour_y)

num_cols = len(grid_lines_x)
num_rows = len(grid_lines_y)

print(f"\nGrid Lines Structure: {num_rows} rows x {num_cols} columns\n")

# find the marked answers using a threshold on the mean value found in gray2
gray4 = gray3.copy()
found_answers = []

for contour in contours:
    mask[:] = 0
    cv2.drawContours(mask, [contour], -1, 255, 2)
    cv2.drawContours(gray4, [contour], -1, (0,255,0), 2)
    
    mean_val = cv2.mean(gray2, mask=mask)[0]
    
    if mean_val < threshold_value:
        M = cv2.moments(contour)
        if M["m00"] != 0:
            cX = int(M["m10"] / M["m00"])
            cY = int(M["m01"] / M["m00"])
        else:
            cX, cY = 0, 0
        found_answers.append({'contour': contour, 'x': cX, 'y': cY, 'mean': mean_val})

# computes row and column indices on the full grid from abs difference 
table1_rows = []
table2_rows = []

for item in found_answers:
    found_x, found_y = item['x'], item['y']
    
    # compute grid lines indices starting with 1 rather than 0
    col_idx = min(range(len(grid_lines_x)), key=lambda i: abs(grid_lines_x[i] - found_x)) + 1
    row_idx = min(range(len(grid_lines_y)), key=lambda i: abs(grid_lines_y[i] - found_y)) + 1
    
    # important: change row index from 10 to 0, since this particular table has 
    # circles labeled as 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,0
    if row_idx == 10:
        row_idx = 0
    
    table1_rows.append([found_x, found_y])
    table2_rows.append([found_x, found_y, row_idx, col_idx])
    
    # draw green contours for found answers on the gray3 image
    cv2.drawContours(gray3, [item['contour']], -1, (0, 255, 0), 2)

# sort table 2 entries by column index first, then row index
table2_rows.sort(key=lambda item: (item[3], item[2]))

# Print a list of Found Answer centers
print("\n--- TABLE 1: List of Answer Centers ---")
print(f"{'Center X':<8} {'Center Y':<8}")
print("-" * 17)
for x, y in table1_rows:
    print(f"{x:<8} {y:<8}")

# print a list of found answer centers and rRow/column indices
print("\n\n--- TABLE 2: Table of Answer Centers & Row/Column Indices ---")
print(f"{'Center X':<8} {'Center Y':<8} {'Row Index':<10} {'Column Index':<10}")
print("-" * 41)
for x, y, row, column in table2_rows:
    print(f"{x:<8} {y:<8} {row:<10} {column:<10}")  

# copy all the row values from Table 2 and print with comma separators
extracted_rows = [str(row) for x, y, row, column in table2_rows]
print("\n--------- List of Row Values --------")
print(", ".join(extracted_rows))

print(f"\n\nCount of All Contours:", len(contours))
print(f"Total Number of Found Answers: {len(table2_rows)}\n")

# save results
cv2.imwrite('omr4_cropped.png', img2)
cv2.imwrite('omr4_gray.png', gray)
cv2.imwrite('omr4_thresh.png', thresh)
cv2.imwrite('omr4_found_contours.png', gray4)
cv2.imwrite('omr4_passed_contours.png', gray3)

# show results
cv2.imshow("cropped", img2)
cv2.imshow("gray", gray)
cv2.imshow("thresh", thresh)
cv2.imshow("found contours", gray4)
cv2.imshow("passed contours", gray3)
cv2.waitKey(0)
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Q: xarray change subset of values of Dataset variable obtained from pandas DataFrame inconsistent with pandas v3 A:

Pandas 3 made Copy-on-Write mandatory. So when pandas exposes a NumPy array that shares memory with a pandas object, the NumPy view is deliberately marked read-only. You can check if that's the case in your code:

print(xrds["lon"].data.flags.writeable)
print(xrds2["lon"].data.flags.writeable)

I would expect this to print False and True respectively.

In your case .fillna could solve this. Instead of indexed assignments, you can convert your replacement Series to an xarray DataArray and let xarray align it by location:

updates = locdf["lon"].to_xarray()
xrds["lon"] = xrds["lon"].fillna(updates)

Note that updates has coordinates location=['b', 'c'], whereas xrds["lon"] has location=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'].

DataArray.fillna() explicitly aligns the replacement DataArray to the calling object using a left join, so the shorter replacement array is matched by its location labels rather than by positional length. So in your case, your two-element replacement is also basically reindexed to the operation you wanted:

a  NaN
b  12.0
c  14.5
d  NaN

So you could directly write:

xrds["lon"] = xrds["lon"].fillna(locdf["lon"].to_xarray())

If you actually want mutable xarray data (e.g. for a lot of in-place operations) then I would break the pandas-owned memory connection explicitly:

xrds["lon"] = xrds["lon"].copy(deep=True)
xrds["lon"].loc[{"location": xrds["lon"].isnull()}] = locdf["lon"]

# or for A TON of variables:
xrds = xrds.copy(deep=True)

Also disclaimer: This works for your example because the subset to be replaced is exactly the set of missing NaN values. If the goal is to replace an arbitrary labelled subset regardless of its current values, fillna would NOT be equivalent

Q: What is the best way to create FTP server in Azure? A:

Using the SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) support for Azure Blob Storage is the simplest, see: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/secure-file-transfer-protocol-support

There are some limitations listed here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/secure-file-transfer-protocol-known-issues

There are other SFPT servers on the Azure Marketplace, the ones I checked were not cheaper. The easiest way to avoid extra costs is just to turn it one when you need to transfer files.
